sections.title: Long and doubled sounds in borrowed words
sections.body: Book 1 covered general Japanese pronunciation — the five vowel sounds, vowel length, and double consonants. Katakana adds one specific wrinkle: because katakana mostly spells foreign loanwords, both of those rules routinely make the difference between two completely unrelated words. In katakana, a lengthened vowel is written with a horizontal bar (ー) called a よこぼう ('horizontal line') — or たてぼう ('vertical line') when the text runs top-to-bottom — rather than by repeating a vowel letter the way hiragana does. Treat that bar as a full extra beat, not a decoration: kora ('hey!') versus koora (cola), bin (bottle) versus biin (bean), and pasu (path) versus paasu (purse) are pairs of genuinely different words that differ only in vowel length. The same goes for doubled consonants: roku (six) versus rokku (rock music), kata (mold/model) versus kataa (cutter), and haka (gravesite) versus hakkaa (hacker) are distinguished only by how long the consonant sound is held. And even though many katakana words started life as English words, always pronounce them the Japanese way — asking for a hoteru, not a 'hotel,' is what actually gets understood.

exercises.prompt: Which pair of words differs only by vowel length?
Which pair of words differs only by a doubled consonant?

'kata' means mold/model. What does 'kataa' (with a doubled consonant) mean?
Match each word to its meaning: rimokon, ranpu, hondana, tansu
Match each word to its meaning: kechappu, masutaado, shouyu, mayoneezu
'hoteru' is the Japanese pronunciation of an English word. Why should you say 'hoteru' instead of an English accent when in Japan?
exercises.answer: Because katakana words are their own Japanese words with fixed pronunciations — using the English pronunciation is likely to not be understood.

points.title: Quick review of regular verb conjugation
points.explanation: From Book 1: the dictionary form of every verb ends in an う-row hiragana. Shifting that final hiragana to its い-row counterpart and attaching an ending builds the four polite forms you already know (~ます, ~ました, ~ません, ~ませんでした).

points.title: What is an いる/える verb?
points.explanation: Most verbs are 'regular' and conjugate the way 1-1 describes. But a second category exists: verbs whose dictionary form ends in る, where the two hiragana right before that る rhyme with い or え. These are called いる/える verbs, and they conjugate differently — instead of shifting the final hiragana to its い-row form, you simply drop る entirely and attach the ending directly.

points.title: The four verb categories
points.explanation: Every Japanese verb falls into one of four categories: (1) Regular verbs — don't end in る, or end in る without the いる/える rhyme. (2) いる/える verbs — end in る with that specific rhyme, conjugated by dropping る. (3) いる/える exception verbs — look like category 2 but are actually conjugated as regular verbs; かえる (to return) is the one you already know. (4) Irregular verbs — くる (to come) and する (to do), which don't follow any pattern and must be memorized individually.

examples.english: to eat -> eat (category 2: いる/える verb)

examples.japanese: かえる → かえります
examples.english: to return -> return (category 3: いる/える exception)

points.title: Don't assume every る-ending verb is an いる/える verb
points.explanation: This is the single most common mistake at this stage. A verb ending in る is only an いる/える verb if the two hiragana immediately before る rhyme with い or え. わかる (to understand) ends in る, but its preceding syllables don't fit that rhyme, so it's a regular verb, not an いる/える verb. When in doubt, check the rhyme, not just the final letter.

examples.japanese: わかる → わかります
examples.english: to understand -> understand (regular, not いる/える)
to eat -> eat (真の いる/える verb, for contrast)

points.title: The particle と as 'with'
points.explanation: You already know と as 'and,' used between two nouns. と has a second job: placed directly after a single noun (not between two), it means 'with.' Context tells you which meaning is intended — と between two nouns is 'and'; と following just one noun is 'with.'

examples.english: I am going with a friend.
dog and cat (the 'and' usage, for comparison)

notes.title: いる — existence for animate things
notes.body: いる is used for anything living and capable of independent movement — people, animals, insects. The thing that exists is marked with が (or は for emphasis/topic), and the location it's in is marked with に, following the pattern '(person/animal) が (place) に います.'

notes.title: ある — existence for inanimate things
notes.body: ある covers everything that isn't animate — objects, plants, buildings — and can mean either 'to have' or 'to be located,' depending on context. It's mostly regular in conjugation, with one quirk: it doesn't have a casual/informal negative form built the normal way, which becomes relevant once casual speech is introduced later in this book.

notes.title: What is a stroke?
notes.body: A stroke is a single continuous mark made without lifting the pen, the same fundamental unit used for hiragana. Katakana characters tend to be more angular than hiragana, built from straight lines rather than curves.

notes.title: Continuous strokes
notes.body: Some katakana characters are conventionally written as a single continuous stroke even where the shape looks like it could be broken into two — following the standard stroke count matters for legibility and for building correct muscle memory, not just for looking 'right.'

notes.title: Writing direction
notes.body: Like hiragana, katakana is written left-to-right and top-to-bottom in modern usage, though top-to-bottom, right-to-left formatting still appears in some published and formal contexts.

notes.title: ほんとう — really, true, truly
notes.body: On its own, ほんとう can ask 'is that true?'. It becomes stronger when paired with に (ほんとうに), letting you intensify an adjective or a whole action — similar to how English uses 'really' before an adjective or verb to add emphasis.

sections.title: A memory trick for aru vs. iru
sections.body: Students commonly mix up ある (inanimate) and いる (animate). One trick: written in romaji, aru starts with A and ends in U, while iru starts with I and ends in U — but if you instead pair them by their vowel pattern, 'aru is for inanimate, iru is for animate' becomes easier to lock in by just remembering the pairing A-I, I-A: the first letter of 'aru' matches the second concept, and vice versa. Any mnemonic that sticks for you personally works just as well.

points.title: Using の to link a location word to a place
points.explanation: の isn't only for possession — it can also mean 'of,' linking a location word (like 'front,' 'behind,' 'inside') to the specific place or object it's relative to.

examples.english: to the right of the desk

points.title: Structuring sentences with あいだ ('between')
points.explanation: To say something is between two items, list both items connected by と, then follow with のあいだ before the location verb.

examples.japanese: かぎはテレビとコンピューターのあいだにあります。
examples.romaji: Kagi wa terebi to konpyuutaa no aida ni arimasu.
examples.english: The keys are between the TV and the computer.

points.title: Using a location phrase to directly modify a noun
points.explanation: Rather than saying 'the book is on the table' as a full sentence, you can fold the location directly into the noun phrase itself — 'the book on top of the table' — using の to connect the location word to the noun that follows it.

examples.japanese: テーブルのうえのほん
examples.english: the book on top of the table

points.title: Combining ひだり and みぎ with other location words
points.explanation: Left and right can stack with other location words to describe a more precise position, the same way English combines 'upper' and 'right' into 'upper right.'

points.title: The difference between となり and そば／よこ
points.explanation: となり is reserved for things of the same category or type sitting next to each other — a house next to another house, a chair next to another chair. そば and よこ are more flexible: they describe physical closeness regardless of whether the two things are the same type of object.

examples.japanese: ぎんこうはゆうびんきょくのとなりにあります。
examples.romaji: Ginkou wa yuubinkyoku no tonari ni arimasu.
examples.english: The bank is next to the post office (same category of thing, so となり).

examples.japanese: ねこはつくえのそばにいます。
examples.romaji: Neko wa tsukue no soba ni imasu.
examples.english: The cat is near the desk (different kinds of things, so そば, not となり).

notes.title: Writing ク and ケ the correct way
notes.body: ク and ケ are easy to mix up when written quickly. The key difference is the second stroke: ク's second stroke is a short diagonal that doesn't cross the first, while ケ has an additional distinct stroke that gives it a more complex, layered shape. Slow down on these two until the difference feels automatic.

points.title: The この group
points.explanation: This lesson introduces four new words — どの (which), この (this), その (that), あの (that over there) — that look similar to どれ/これ/それ/あれ from Book 1, but work differently: they can never stand alone. Every word in this group must be immediately followed by the noun it describes.

points.title: どれ vs. どの, and the rest of the pattern
points.explanation: The どれ/これ/それ/あれ group (from Book 1) stands completely on its own and can never be placed directly in front of a noun. The どの/この/その/あの group does the opposite — it can never stand alone and must always attach to a noun. Mixing the two up is one of the most common beginner errors at this stage, so it's worth deliberately practicing both patterns side by side.

examples.japanese: これはなんですか。 ／ このほんはなんですか。
examples.romaji: Kore wa nan desu ka. / Kono hon wa nan desu ka.
examples.english: What is this? / What is this book? (standalone vs. attributive)

notes.title: Stroke order differences for シ (shi) and ソ (so)
notes.body: シ and ソ are near-mirror images of each other and are frequently confused. The distinguishing detail is stroke direction: シ's two short strokes angle from upper-left toward lower-right, while ソ's strokes angle from upper-right toward lower-left. Writing them at speed with the correct stroke order — not just the correct final shape — is what makes the difference stick.

sections.title: Guessing gender from a name
sections.body: Japanese given names often hint at gender through their ending sound, though it's never a certainty. Names ending in こ are very commonly female, and names ending in ろ or し are very commonly male — but there are enough exceptions on both sides that asking directly is always the safer move if it matters.

sections.title: A counting song for the people counter
sections.body: Some learners find it easier to memorize the people counter (ひとり、ふたり、さんにん...) by setting it to a simple, familiar counting-song rhythm — the same trick used for memorizing multiplication tables or the alphabet. Any tune with a steady, repetitive beat works; the goal is just muscle memory through repetition, not the specific song itself.

points.title: Connecting sentences with そして
points.explanation: そして means 'and,' but unlike と (which only joins items in a list), そして joins two complete sentences together, always starting the second sentence.

examples.japanese: きのうはいそがしかったです。そして、きょうもいそがしいです。
examples.romaji: Kinou wa isogashikatta desu. Soshite, kyou mo isogashii desu.
examples.english: Yesterday was busy. And, today is busy too.

points.title: The same idea, said several different ways
points.explanation: As your Japanese grows, you'll notice the same question or statement can be phrased several different ways — different particles, different word order, even different verbs — without a real change in meaning. This can feel destabilizing after Book 1's more rigid patterns, but it's completely normal; every language allows this kind of variation, and getting comfortable hearing (and producing) more than one 'correct' phrasing is part of sounding natural rather than textbook-stiff.

points.title: The difference between いる, ある, and です
points.explanation: いる, ある, and です can all translate to English 'is/am/are' in different contexts, but です can never mean 'to have' — only いる and ある can express possession. When asking 'where is it,' です works for anything, ある is limited to inanimate things, and いる is limited to animate things.

points.title: The particle を
points.explanation: Every new verb in this lesson uses を, the direct object marker. を always follows whatever is receiving the action of the verb — the thing being eaten, bought, or sold — no matter where that word falls in the sentence.

points.title: The particle で as an event location marker
points.explanation: で means 'in,' 'at,' or 'on' depending on context, and marks where an event or action (eating, buying, drinking) takes place — distinct from に, which marks the location of a static existence (where something simply is).

examples.japanese: レストランでたべます。
examples.english: I will eat at a restaurant.

examples.japanese: ひこうきでのみました。

points.title: Particle review
points.explanation: This is a good checkpoint to review every particle covered so far: か (question marker), は (topic marker), が (subject/emphasis marker), の (possession/description), と (and / with), も (also/too), に (time/place/destination marker), から (from — starting point), まで (until — ending point), で (event location marker).

examples.japanese: わたしはがくせいです。
examples.english: I am a student. (は — topic marker)

examples.japanese: こうえんにいぬがいます。
examples.english: There is a dog in the park. (に — place; が — subject)

points.title: How much one particle can change a sentence
points.explanation: Swapping a single particle in an otherwise identical sentence can produce a wildly different — sometimes nonsensical — meaning. It's a useful (if slightly absurd) exercise to deliberately swap particles in a sentence you know and see how far the meaning drifts, since it builds a sharper instinct for what each particle is actually doing.

notes.title: 書く — to write
notes.body: The thing being written is marked with を. If a letter is being written to a specific person, that person is marked with に.

points.title: When もう means 'already'

points.title: When もう means 'more'

points.title: When もう means 'anymore'

sections.title: Family terms shift with the youngest member's viewpoint
sections.body: Japanese families often address each other based on the perspective of the youngest child in the household, not from a fixed adult viewpoint. Parents with one child might call each other by affectionate nickname-like terms early on; once a second child arrives, older siblings become 'older brother/sister' to match how the newest child sees them; and once grandchildren exist, the parents themselves shift to being addressed as 'grandfather/grandmother' most of the time, even by their own adult children.

points.title: Using よく to mean 'often'
points.explanation: よく means 'often' and is placed directly before a positive verb.

points.title: Using あまり with negative verbs
points.explanation: You already know あまり as 'not that much.' Paired with a negative verb, it means 'not that often' — functioning as the natural opposite of よく.

examples.japanese: あまりえいがをみません。
examples.english: I don't watch movies that often.

points.title: Making family words sound affectionate
points.explanation: Family terms ending in さん often shift to a cuter, more affectionate form when the speaker is young or wants to sound endearing — commonly by swapping さん for ちゃん, and sometimes shortening the word itself. This isn't universal across every family term, so it's worth learning case by case rather than assuming the swap always applies.

examples.japanese: おにいさん → おにいちゃん
おばあさん → おばあちゃん

points.title: Three types of Japanese adjectives
points.explanation: い-adjectives all end in い and attach directly to the noun they modify with nothing in between. な-adjectives require な inserted between the adjective and the noun it modifies — きれい (pretty) needs きれいな車 ('a pretty car'), not きれい車. の-adjectives are ordinary nouns turned into a modifier by inserting の, the same pattern used for possession — 日本の車 means 'a Japanese car.' One trap worth noting: きれい looks like an い-adjective since it ends in い, but it's actually a な-adjective — one of the few exceptions worth memorizing individually.

points.title: Making い-adjectives past tense
points.explanation: Drop the final い from an い-adjective and add かった to make it past tense — this applies to both the positive and negative forms.

examples.japanese: ふるい → ふるかった
ふるくない → ふるくなかった

points.title: Saying something hurts
points.explanation: 痛い (painful) is an ordinary い-adjective, but it's most commonly used to mean 'hurts' when describing a body part — and since it's an adjective, it follows the normal past-tense and negative conjugation rules like any other い-adjective.

examples.japanese: きのう、あしがいたかったです。

points.title: Connecting sentences with それに

notes.title: 洗う (to wash), 拾う (to pick up)
notes.body: Both verbs mark the thing being washed or picked up with を, following the standard object-marking pattern. 拾う specifically covers 'picking up' in the sense of retrieving an object off the ground, or picking someone up in a vehicle.

points.title: Why informal verb forms matter
points.explanation: Every polite form learned so far (~ます, ~ました, etc.) has a casual/informal counterpart used with close friends and family, and mastering it is essential to sounding genuinely fluent rather than textbook-formal. This lesson introduces how to derive every informal form directly from a verb's dictionary form.

examples.english: eat (polite) -> eat (informal, used with close friends/family)

examples.japanese: いきません → いかない

points.title: The informal present/future form you already know
points.explanation: The dictionary form of a verb IS its informal present/future form — the same form you'd look a verb up by. Context (time words, or the flow of conversation) determines whether it's read as present or future tense, since Japanese doesn't grammatically separate the two the way English does.

examples.japanese: あした、がっこうにいく。
examples.english: I'll go to school tomorrow. (future, from context)

examples.japanese: まいにち、がっこうにいく。
examples.english: I go to school every day. (present, from context)

points.title: The informal negative (ない form)
points.explanation: For regular verbs, shift the final う-row hiragana to its あ-row counterpart and add ない. For いる/える verbs, simply drop る and add ない — the same drop-and-attach logic used for their polite forms.

points.title: Special rule for verbs ending in う
points.explanation: Verbs whose dictionary form ends in う (rather than shifting to あ as expected) shift to わ instead when forming the informal negative — a small but important irregularity worth memorizing on its own.

examples.japanese: あらう → あらわない

points.title: Irregular verbs in the informal negative
points.explanation: くる (to come), する (to do), and ある (to be/exist, inanimate) each have their own irregular informal negative form that must be memorized rather than derived from a rule.

points.title: The た-form (informal past)
points.explanation: The informal past tense is called the た-form, because it always ends in た or だ. It is built by changing the verb's final hiragana according to a set of sound-based rules. These are the same rules as the て-form you will meet later, with た/だ in place of て/で, so it's worth practicing them until they're automatic. For いる/える verbs, swap the final る for た (たべる → たべた). For う-verbs, the ending decides: う, つ and る become った (かう → かった, まつ → まった, とる → とった); む, ぶ and ぬ become んだ (のむ → のんだ, あそぶ → あそんだ, しぬ → しんだ); く becomes いた (かく → かいた); ぐ becomes いだ (およぐ → およいだ); す becomes した (はなす → はなした). いく (to go) is the one exception among く-verbs: it becomes いった. The two irregular verbs are する → した and くる → きた.

notes.title: Turning an informal statement into a question
notes.body: Attaching か after an informal verb form works exactly like the polite です/ます + か pattern, but informal か is rarely used in writing — it's a spoken-conversation tool, said with a rising intonation, and should never be used toward someone of higher social standing (a boss, a teacher).

notes.title: Using よ for emphasis
notes.body: Ending a statement (not a question) with よ, said without rising intonation, adds emphasis or emotional weight to what you're saying. It's more commonly used by women in casual speech; men tend to reach for ぜ or just the plain informal verb form instead when making a similarly emphatic statement.

notes.title: The particle ね
notes.body: ね at the end of a sentence functions something like an exclamation point, adding emotion, certainty, or a sense of shared agreement/confirmation with the listener. Said in a neutral tone it barely changes the meaning; said with more emphasis, it can come across as quite assertive.

sections.title: Where the name Godzilla came from
sections.body: The Japanese name for Godzilla is a blend of two existing words: one meaning 'whale' and one meaning 'gorilla,' combined into a single new word. The English name 'Godzilla' is a separate adaptation of that blended Japanese name, not a direct translation of it.

notes.title: 見る (to see/watch), 聞く (to listen/ask/hear)
notes.body: Both verbs mark the thing being watched or listened to with を, following the same object-marking pattern as every other transitive verb learned so far. 見る is an いる/える-type verb; 聞く is regular.

points.title: Connecting sentences with から ('because')
points.explanation: から joins a reason (sentence 1) to a result (sentence 2) — sentence 1 is always the cause, sentence 2 is always the effect, regardless of which English word ('because,' 'since,' 'so') you'd use to translate it.

examples.japanese: おかねがないから、えいがにいきません。
examples.romaji: Okane ga nai kara, eiga ni ikimasen.
examples.english: Because I have no money, I'm not going to the movies.

points.title: Choosing verb formality across a から sentence
points.explanation: Sentence 1 sounds most natural in informal form; the overall politeness of the whole statement is set by sentence 2's form. Both sentences can be informal, or sentence 1 can be informal with sentence 2 polite — but sentence 1 can never be more polite than sentence 2. Think of it as 'formality can only go up, never down' across the から boundary.

examples.japanese: さむいから、まどをしめます。
examples.english: Because it's cold, I'll close the window. (clause 1 informal, clause 2 polite — allowed)

examples.japanese: さむいですから、まどをしめます。
examples.romaji: Samui desu kara, mado wo shimemasu.
examples.english: Because it's cold, I'll close the window. (both clauses polite — also allowed)

points.title: What happens to です before から
points.explanation: If sentence 1 ends in an い-adjective, です is simply dropped before から. If sentence 1 ends in a な-adjective or a noun, です shifts to its informal form だ before から.

examples.japanese: あついから、プールにいきます。
examples.english: Because it's hot, I'll go to the pool. (い-adjective: です dropped)

examples.japanese: きれいだから、すきです。
examples.english: Because it's pretty, I like it. (な-adjective: です → だ)

points.title: Using どんな ('what kind of')
points.explanation: どんな behaves exactly like どの (from Book 2, Lesson 3) — it can never stand alone and must always be immediately followed by a noun.

examples.japanese: どんなおんがくがすきですか。
examples.romaji: Donna ongaku ga suki desu ka.
examples.english: What kind of music do you like?

notes.title: The 33 compound katakana are built from characters you already know
notes.body: Every compound katakana sound is formed by combining a full-size katakana with a small ゃ/ゅ/ょ (or ャ/ュ/ョ in katakana form) — the exact same combining principle as compound hiragana. If you can already read the base katakana, you can sound out any compound on sight.

notes.title: Writing compound katakana correctly
notes.body: As with compound hiragana, the second character in a compound katakana pair must be written visibly smaller than the first — writing both at full size turns one combined sound into two separate syllables.

notes.title: The word-separator dot (・)
notes.body: When two or more katakana words appear back-to-back — most often in foreign names — a small dot is sometimes placed between them to mark where one word ends and the next begins. It's optional, but it noticeably improves readability, especially with longer foreign names.

points.title: Conjugating する and です
points.explanation: する and です are both irregular verbs and don't follow any conjugation pattern taught so far — their forms simply need to be memorized individually. です is not an action verb (it doesn't describe doing something), so its English translations differ slightly from a typical verb's (is/was/isn't/wasn't rather than do/did/don't/didn't).

examples.japanese: する → します → しません → しました → しませんでした
examples.english: to do -> do/will do -> don't/won't do -> did -> didn't do

examples.japanese: です → ではありません

points.title: Creating new verbs with する
points.explanation: Attaching する directly after many nouns turns them into a verb — 'to do [noun].' This is an extremely productive pattern in Japanese; a huge number of verbs, especially newer or borrowed ones, are built this way rather than existing as a standalone dictionary verb.

examples.japanese: べんきょう+する → べんきょうする

points.title: Using を with する verbs
points.explanation: When the noun-plus-する pattern describes doing something to or with a specific thing, を can be inserted between the noun and する, marking that noun as the object.

points.title: Asking 'how much' with する
points.explanation: する has a second meaning beyond 'to do' — it can also mean 'to cost.' Combined with いくら (how much), いくらします か asks how much something costs, functioning as a natural alternative to いくらですか.

examples.japanese: これはいくらしますか。

example_words.japanese: ファミリーレストラン

notes.title: Why these compounds exist
notes.body: Standard katakana can represent every native Japanese sound, but foreign words often contain sounds that don't fit neatly into that set — an 'f' before a vowel other than 'u,' or a 'd' before 'i,' for example. This lesson's compounds (built the same way as the standard compounds, but paired with different small vowel characters) exist specifically to represent those foreign sounds more accurately than the standard katakana set alone could.

points.title: Using まだ
points.explanation: まだ means 'not yet' or 'still,' and can pair with either positive or negative words. Generally (though not as a strict rule), まだ with a negative word means 'not yet,' and まだ with a positive word means 'still.'

points.title: Making a specific time less specific with くらい／ぐらい
points.explanation: くらい (or ぐらい) means 'around' or 'about,' and always comes directly after the time it's softening.

examples.japanese: じゅういちじぐらいにいきます。
examples.english: I will go around eleven o'clock.

points.title: Making a specific amount less specific with くらい／ぐらい
points.explanation: The same くらい／ぐらい also softens amounts and durations, not just points in time — it can make any exact quantity approximate.

examples.japanese: いちじかんぐらいべんきょうします。
examples.english: I will study for about an hour.
